blocks.text: Quick verdict

Proxy-Cheap is the better choice for low-cost work on easier targets: about $7.80 for 10 GB at its promotional rate against $80 at Bright Data's list price, with no subscription and SOCKS5 with UDP. Bright Data is the better choice for hardened targets, precise geo work and enterprise pipelines, where its pool depth, ZIP, ASN and carrier targeting, Web Unlocker and compliance processes prevent costly failures. Many teams route easy pages through a budget network and reserve Bright Data for the hard ones.

Bright Data and Proxy-Cheap sit at opposite ends of the residential proxy market. Bright Data is the premium enterprise platform with a 150M+ pool, ZIP and carrier targeting and managed unblocking products. Proxy-Cheap is a budget shop currently advertising rotating residential traffic at $0.78/GB with no plan. The price gap at small volumes is roughly tenfold, so this comparison is about which workloads need Bright Data's capabilities and which are better served by cheap bandwidth.

blocks.text: Bright Data in 2026: what you get

Bright Data is the largest and most complete web-data platform in this market. Beyond residential proxies it sells datacenter, ISP and mobile networks, an unblocking API, a SERP API, a hosted Scraping Browser and ready-made datasets, each billed on its own meter. Its residential network is advertised at more than 150 million IPs in 195 countries, with targeting down to ZIP code and ASN. The trade-off is cost and complexity: the list price sits at the top of the market and the dashboard is built around zones, rules and compliance checks rather than a two-click setup.

Strengths: Deepest targeting in the market (ZIP, ASN, carrier); Managed unblocking, SERP and browser products under one account; Mature compliance and KYC processes that enterprise buyers ask for; Very large residential pool for high-rotation work. Weak spots: Highest list price per GB at low volume; Dashboard and zone setup take time to learn; Some targets need a compliance review before access.
Proxy-Cheap in 2026: what you get

Proxy-Cheap has sold proxies since 2018 and says it serves 45,000+ customers. It offers seven product types: static residential (ISP) in IPv4 and IPv6, rotating residential, datacenter IPv4 and IPv6, and static and rotating mobile. Rotating residential is pure pay-as-you-go with no monthly plan, and the site claims coverage in 180+ countries. Targeting is mainly country and ISP level, and all products support SOCKS5 including UDP. It is a strong value pick, though independent benchmarks of its rotating pool have been mixed.

Strengths: Very low per-GB price while the promotion runs; No monthly commitment on rotating residential; Broad catalog including IPv6 and static mobile; SOCKS5 with UDP support. Weak spots: Targeting is mostly country and ISP, not city; Residential pool size not separately published; Mixed results in some independent benchmarks.
Pricing: Bright Data vs Proxy-Cheap

Bright Data lists residential traffic at $8/GB pay-as-you-go with no commitment, and it frequently runs 50%-off promotions that bring that to about $4/GB. Monthly plans start with the Growth tier at $499 for roughly 141 GB (about $3.50/GB) and fall to around $2.50/GB on the largest public plan.

Proxy-Cheap's rotating residential proxies are pay-as-you-go, currently listed from $0.78/GB (a promotional price against a $2.60/GB list rate). Static residential ISP proxies start around $2.44 per IP per month, datacenter IPv4 at about $1.49, datacenter IPv6 from $0.15, and rotating mobile at $5.99/GB.

At 10 GB a month, Proxy-Cheap is the cheaper option at about $7.80 against $80 for Bright Data, roughly 90% less. Buying 100 GB, you would pay about $78 with Proxy-Cheap and $499 with Bright Data: a 84% saving in Proxy-Cheap's favour. Both Bright Data and Proxy-Cheap work on allowances that do not carry forward indefinitely, so size your plan to real monthly usage rather than buying ahead.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

Proxy-Cheap does not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. Bright Data lists '150M+' and Proxy-Cheap lists 'Not separately published (155M+ claimed across all products)'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, Bright Data lists 195 countries and Proxy-Cheap lists 180+. On targeting, Bright Data offers country, state, city, ZIP, ASN and carrier, while Proxy-Cheap offers country and ISP.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, Bright Data offers rotating per request or sticky sessions you control per zone, and Proxy-Cheap offers rotating and sticky sessions. Setup works the same way on both: a single gateway endpoint, with location and session options passed as username parameters, plus IP whitelisting if you prefer not to use credentials.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: Bright Data. Bright Data has the edge here. Why: its pool depth and Web Unlocker handle hardened targets. How Proxy-Cheap compares: cheap traffic, though independent benchmark results have been mixed.
SERP and rank tracking: Bright Data. Bright Data has the edge here. Why: it sells a dedicated SERP API alongside raw proxies. How Proxy-Cheap compares: workable for light rank tracking at a low cost.

Social media and multi-account management: Proxy-Cheap. Proxy-Cheap has the edge here. Why: cheap static ISP and mobile IPs for persistent identities. How Bright Data compares: it is powerful but expensive for low-volume account work.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: Bright Data wins. The deciding factor for Bright Data: ZIP-level targeting suits local pricing and stock checks. The limitation on the Proxy-Cheap side: fine for country-level price checks.

Ad verification and geo-testing: Bright Data wins. The deciding factor for Bright Data: carrier and ASN targeting reproduce what real users see. The limitation on the Proxy-Cheap side: lacks city-level targeting on rotating residential.
Tight budgets: Proxy-Cheap. Proxy-Cheap has the edge here. Why: the lowest advertised per-GB price in this pairing. How Bright Data compares: its list price is the highest in this comparison.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. Bright Data: Free trial for business accounts, no card required. Proxy-Cheap: 7-day $1.99 trial on static residential and datacenter IPs. Verification and payment rules differ too. Bright Data: Verification required for some sensitive targets. Proxy-Cheap: Light; card, PayPal, Alipay and crypto accepted. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test Bright Data and Proxy-Cheap before you commit
Spec sheets only get you so far. A short, structured test on your own targets will settle Bright Data vs Proxy-Cheap faster than any review:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (Bright Data: free trial for business accounts, no card required; Proxy-Cheap: 7-day $1.99 trial on static residential and datacenter IPs).

2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day. 3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, Bright Data comes out ahead in 4, Proxy-Cheap in 2, and 0 are ties. That makes Bright Data the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: Bright Data is strongest for enterprise data teams with budget for managed tooling, while Proxy-Cheap is strongest for price-sensitive scraping at moderate difficulty. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
